newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lawyers appeal on line-item veto ruling.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lawyers appeal on line-item veto ruling.

text.p: The Clinton administration Friday urged the Supreme Court to uphold the constitutionality of a new law that greatly expanded presidential veto power.

In a 27-page appeal, Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger asked the high court to hear the case and to overturn a federal judge's ruling declaring the historic line-item veto law unconstitutional.

The court papers were filed a week after President Clinton announced a quick Supreme Court appeal in an attempt to reinstate the law, which gives the president the power to strip items from spending measures without vetoing a whole bill.

Presidents of both parties had long coveted line-item veto power because it vastly expands their room for manoeuvre in budgetary matters and has been viewed as a powerful tool to reduce the federal budget deficit.
The law was enacted last year by the Republican Congress as part of its Contract with America and was strongly supported by Clinton, who has yet to use it since it went into effect in January.
The law was challenged in court by six members of Congress, who claimed it violated the processes laid out by the Constitution.
Dellinger first made the procedural argument that the individual members of Congress lacked legal standing to bring the lawsuit in the first place.

"Members of Congress have no judicially cognizable interest in the operation or the outcome of the legislative process. Judicial intervention is particularly unwarranted where, as here, the president has yet to take any action that is claimed to offend" the Constitution, he said.
The second argument by Dellinger, the administration's top courtroom lawyer, was that the justices should uphold the law if they decide to reach the merits of the case.
"The act is simply the latest exercise of Congress's longstanding and well-settled power to vest the executive branch with discretion over the expenditure of appropriated funds," he said.

"The Line Item Veto Act is no different from any other federal statute that gives the president discretion to decide whether or not to expend funds that have been appropriated by Congress," Dellinger said.
If the Supreme Court agrees to hear the appeal, both sides in the dispute have recommended that oral arguments be held late in May, with a decision expected by the end of June.
